label: Projective Planes
notes: Open by framing the chapter as a move from measurement to incidence. Perspective drawing motivates the whole apparatus: lines stay lines and incidences survive even when distance and parallelism do not. Tell students the destination is three axioms, a duality principle, and the seven-point Fano plane.

label: Perspective Preserves Incidence
notes: Stress that central projection forgets lengths, angles, and parallelism but keeps which points lie on which lines. The notebook backs each drawing with a residual check, so a near miss in the picture is never mistaken for a theorem. The vanishing point is the visual seed of an ideal point.

label: The Line at Infinity
notes: Explain that we cure parallelism by adding one ideal point per direction class and collecting all ideal points on a single line at infinity. Emphasise this is a data rule, not a drawing trick. Parallel Euclidean lines now meet at their shared ideal point, so exceptions to the meet axiom disappear.

label: Axioms of a Projective Plane
notes: State the three incidence axioms carefully. A1 and A2 are exact mirror images under swapping point and line. A3 forbids degenerate collapses by demanding four points in general position. Make clear that no metric appears anywhere; the plane is defined purely by an incidence relation between two kinds of object.

label: No Parallels
notes: Contrast Euclid's parallel postulate with axiom A2: in a projective plane every two distinct lines meet, so parallel lines simply do not exist. Walk through why the join and meet are unique, citing the no-double-incidence lemma that stops two points from sharing two lines and keeps the counting honest.

label: The Principle of Duality
notes: Introduce duality as the deepest structural symmetry of the subject. Because A1 and A2 swap into each other and A3 is self-dual, any theorem stated in incidence terms yields a valid dual theorem by trading the words point and line, join and meet. Promise that later chapters exploit this to halve their work.

label: Counting in a Finite Plane
notes: Derive the order-n counting result. Fix a point, count lines through it, count points per line, and the no-double-incidence lemma prevents overcounting. Every line carries n+1 points and every point meets n+1 lines, giving n squared plus n plus one points and equally many lines. Order two yields seven.

label: Building the Fano Plane
notes: Show the construction concretely. Start from the four general-position points A3 guarantees; their joins give six lines; opposite line pairs meet in three new points; the meet axiom forces one final line through those three. Counting closes at seven points and seven lines, the smallest projective plane, of order two.

label: The Fano Plane Diagram
notes: Walk the figure point by point. The triangle vertices, edge midpoints, and centre give seven points; six straight lines plus the curved circle line make seven lines. Stress that the curve through the midpoints is a drawing convention for one abstract three-point line; the incidence table, not the picture, is the real model.

label: Incidence Table and Self-Duality
notes: Present the seven-by-seven incidence matrix. Rows are points, columns are lines, a one marks incidence. Transposing swaps the roles of points and lines, and every uniqueness test still passes, so the Fano plane is self-dual. This transpose is the cleanest computational witness of the duality principle in action.

label: Orders and Existence
notes: Survey the landscape of finite planes. Planes of order two, three, four, and five exist; order six does not, by Bruck-Ryser. The existence question for general orders is open and famously hard. Mention that all known finite projective planes have prime-power order, which students should treat as a striking unsolved pattern.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Recap the five load-bearing ideas: keep incidence, perspective explains why, ideal points remove parallels, point and line are dual, and the Fano plane is minimal. Point ahead to homogeneous coordinates in Chapter 3, which turn these synthetic axioms into linear algebra over a field and make computation routine.
